Recall that for any 2×2 real matrix A with complex eigenvalues, we have A=PCP−1, where

P=[||Re(v)Im(v)||],C=[Re(λ)Im(λ)−Im(λ)Re(λ)],

and v is an eigenvector of A corresponding to the complex eigenvalue λ.

To compute the eigenvalues of A, we solve the characteristic equation, as follows: det(A−λI)=0|2−λ1−13−4−λ|=0λ2+2λ+5=0 Using the quadratic formula, we get λ=−b±b2−4ac2a=−1±2i.

Let's consider the eigenvalue λ=−1−2i. We can immediately construct the rotation-scaling matrix:

C=[−1−22−1]

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation (A−λI)x=0. In our case, we have λ1=−1−2i, and

A−λI=[21−13−4]−[−1−2i00−1−2i]=[3+2i1−13−3+2i].

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

{(3+2i)x1+x2=0−13x1+(−3+2i)x2=0.

Since the matrix A−λI is singular, the system above has a non-trivial solution. This implies that one row is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as free. For example, from the first equation, we get

x2=(−3−2i)x1

content.knowledge_point: Converting a Matrix to Rotation-Scaling Form Given Only One Eigenvalue
content.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -13 & -4\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}a & b \\ c & d\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above.
Given that $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where $C$ is a rotation-scaling matrix, what is the value of 
$\frac{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}{{c}^{2}+{d}^{2}}?$
content.worked_solution:
Recall that for any $2\times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}],
$$

and $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue  $\lambda .$

To compute the eigenvalues of $A,$ we solve the characteristic equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}2-\lambda  & 1 \\ -13 & -4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+2\lambda +5 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a}=-1\pm 2\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's consider the eigenvalue $\lambda =-1-2\text{i}.$ We can immediately construct the rotation-scaling matrix:

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -2 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 
$(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.$ 
In our case, we have $\,{\lambda }_{1}=-1-2\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -13 & -4\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-1-2\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -1-2\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3+2\text{i} & 1 \\ -13 & -3+2\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(3+2\text{i}){x}_{1}+{x}_{2}=0 \\ -13{x}_{1}+(-3+2\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the matrix $A-\lambda I$ is singular, the system above has a non-trivial solution. This implies that one row is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as free. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=(-3-2\text{i}){x}_{1}
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ (-3-2\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1$, we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -3-2\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we can construct the matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -3 & -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
\frac{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}{{c}^{2}+{d}^{2}}=\frac{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}}{(-3)^{2}+(-2)^{2}}=\frac{1}{13}.
$$

content.knowledge_point: Converting a Matrix to Rotation-Scaling Form Given Only One Eigenvalue
content.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ -5 & -1\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}a & b \\ c & d\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above.
Given that $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where $C$ is a rotation-scaling matrix, what is the value of 
$\frac{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}{{c}^{2}+{d}^{2}}?$
content.worked_solution:
Recall that for any $2\times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}],
$$

and $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue  $\lambda .$

To compute the eigenvalues of $A,$ we solve the characteristic equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-3-\lambda  & 2 \\ -5 & -1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+4\lambda +13 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a}=-2\pm 3\text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's consider the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2+3\text{i}.$ We can immediately construct the rotation-scaling matrix:

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 3 \\ -3 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 
$(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.$ 
In our case, we have $\,{\lambda }_{1}=-2+3\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ -5 & -1\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-2+3\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -2+3\text{i}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1-3\text{i} & 2 \\ -5 & 1-3\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(-1-3\text{i}){x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0 \\ -5{x}_{1}+(1-3\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the matrix $A-\lambda I$ is singular, the system above has a non-trivial solution. This implies that one row is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as free. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{5}(1-3\text{i}){x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}(1-3\text{i}){x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=5$, we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}1-3\text{i} \\ 5\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we can construct the matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -3 \\ 5 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\frac{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}{{c}^{2}+{d}^{2}}=\frac{{1}^{2}+(-3)^{2}}{{5}^{2}+{0}^{2}}=\frac{2}{5}.
$$

content.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ -10 & -9\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}a & b \\ c & d\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above.
Given that $A$ has the complex eigenvalue $\lambda =-3+2\text{i},$ and that $A=PC{P}^{-1}$ where $C$ is a rotation-scaling matrix, what is the value of 
$\frac{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}{{c}^{2}+{d}^{2}}?$
content.worked_solution:
Recall that for any $2\times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}],
$$

and $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue  $\lambda .$

Since we are given the eigenvalue $\lambda =-3+2\text{i},$ we can immediately construct the rotation-scaling matrix:

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ -2 & -3\end{aligned}]
$$

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,{\lambda }_{1}=-3+2\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 4 \\ -10 & -9\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-3+2\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -3+2\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}6-2\text{i} & 4 \\ -10 & -6-2\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(6-2\text{i}){x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}=0 \\ -10{x}_{1}+(-6-2\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the matrix $A-\lambda I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=\frac{1}{2}(-3+\text{i}){x}_{1}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ \frac{1}{2}(-3+\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=2$, we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3+\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we can construct the matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ -3 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
\frac{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}{{c}^{2}+{d}^{2}}=\frac{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}}{(-3)^{2}+{1}^{2}}=\frac{2}{5}.
$$
